items.title: Theatre Review: Beauty and the Beast (The Firebird Theatre) [FINAL FANTASY XIV Online]
items.summary: I attended The Firebird Theatre's performance of "Beauty and the Beast", and I found a wonderful show fit for any Warrior of Light to enjoy.
items.content:
You can check out The Firebird Theatre at their official website , on YouTube and Twitch, on X and Bluesky , and on Discord .

They are located on the Faerie server, Aether data center, Empyreum Ward 6, Plot 60.

Their next production, The Simple Life of Johanna Cadieu, has not released a performance schedule yet.

After FINAL FANTASY XIV Online first launched with 1.0 on September 30, 2010, and then A Realm Reborn swept out the Seventh Umbral Era and ushed in the Seventh Astral Era in 2013, Eorzea has never been short of stories. There are tales of the faraway lands, legends about Louisoix and the Scions of the Seventh Dawn, and (of course) myths about a star-renowned detective and his assistant. On Faerie server, however, a troupe of performers have decided to bring their own stories to life as part of The Firebird Theatre over in Empyreum ward 6, plot 60.

Last week was the closing series of shows for their seventh (yes, SEVENTH) show, Beauty and the Beast . Scoot Patoot (director, scriptwriter, casting director, and acting consultant) returned to bring this production of a classic fairy tale to life — and this version is not a Disney singalong. During the nearly two-hour runtime (with an intermission partway through), you are introduced to Belle. Expertly portrayed by C’khes “Kel” Rhel, Belle is a woman who wants to take care of her father, stay friends with her pal Vittorio (Leo Stella), and live her life on her own terms. That is, until Marceau (Alexander Shay) is forced to take refuge at a castle during a storm. That castle belongs to the Beast (Stanzek Rosyasch in their first leading role), who was transformed from being a prince (Solace Valjann) by a Pixie (Devil Knight, also in their first production). Rounding out the cast is Jean (Sasu Arkwright) and Gabriel (Romarique De Durendaire) who have been turned invisible because of the Pixie’s curse.

The Firebird Theatre put on their entire performance of Beauty and the Beast inside of their house on the Faerie server. One thing that really surprised me about attending was that they do not sell tickets. Instead, they are a first-come-first served lineup outside of the house. I showed up about an hour-and-a-half early before the matinee performance, and I was nowhere near one of the first people in line. They will let people line up until there is no more room permitted inside, and then they will cut the line off. You are invited to go inside the property via /tell. If you are too late to get inside, the performances are streamed live on Twitch .

Once you’re inside, and after you pass by the interior photo opportunity and jump up the white ‘stairs’ and pass by the concessions area, you enter into a large raised-box theater. For this performance at least, the entire area is covered in flowers on the sides and in the boxed seating, and the floor itself is covered in wood. Somehow, The Firebird Theatre has created a great approximation of a real-life theater. I walked around and tried sitting at various spots in the boxed seating, and I was pleased to find there wasn’t a bad seat in the house to see the show. The Saturday AM performance was the first time I had attended a virtual theatre performance, so I quickly settled myself down into my seat to enjoy the show. I will note that before the show, one of the troupe members was kind enough to pop out and tell everyone what settings to set to ensure that they have the best possible experience.

The acting in The Firebird Theatre’s interpretation of Beauty and the Beast is quite sublime. The characters take full advantage of the space opened up to them on stage and emotes are utilized to really accent the dialogue. As the story progresses, it is hard to not fall in love with the budding romance between Belle and Beast. In fact, Beast honestly kept stealing the show away as his awkward, yet endearing attempts to romance Belle after almost immediately proposing to her make up the heart of the story.

The showstopping moment that really caught my breath, though, was the ballroom dance scene. Romarique De Durendaire (doubling up also as a costume designer) and Altari Arulaq (costume designer) really put together the perfect outfits for both Belle and Beast that made it feel like they stepped out of, well, a fairy tale. Smartly, the ballroom dance is presented as two Dancer jobs pairing up and performing together as Beast teaches Belle how to dance to A Dream in Flight by Masashi Hamauzu. It is simply impossible to not root for these characters, even as Vittorio turns unintentionally foul after a conversation with Marceau, and he tries to kill Beast towards the end of the play before Belle has to step in. Jean and Gabriel, even though they are both played more for comic relief than anything else (and Gabriel doubles up as the narrator), are still entertaining to watch interact with each other and the Beast as he plays a foil for them.

Of course, the set design by Aleu Lyehga is worth mentioning. It blows my mind how every time the ‘curtain’ fell and then raised (which turned the area in front of the audience box ‘black’), the stage itself would be completely different. I was shocked to see everything from a tall flower wall with a bench to a large metal cage to even a long table elaborately laid out for dinner that was effortlessly shuffled in and out quickly to tell the story without missing a (story)beat.

The story, adapted and directed for the Eorzean stage by Scoot Patoot, is tightly written, and the performance time really did fly by in under two hours. I think if there was one issue I had with the show, it is that I did not understand that Gabriel and Jean were both invisible until something was explicitly said later on. I could tell they were both see-through, but it didn’t ‘click’ in my head of what they truly were when they were first on stage. This is, ultimately, a minor issue with the writing that could have been sorted out with a single throwaway line much earlier.

Midway through the show, you were given time to purchase refreshments ranging from a rolanberry for 100 gil to Pixieberry Cheesecake and Rolanberry Shaved Ice for 2,500 gil. Additionally, you can buy Carnations for 10,000 gil, Gridanian Bouquet for 500,000 gil, dried orange/red oldroses for 50,000 gil a pop afterwards outside of the theatre house. I will note that you aren’t guilted into buying anything by the troupe, and it was because of that that I ended up buying a Dried Orange Oldrose afterwards to remember the show.

If you’ve done everything in Eorzea that you can possibly think of right now, and you are just biding your time until you see what Naoki Yoshida is coming up with for the Evercold expansion releasing in January 2027 (or even if you aren’t done with Dawntrail yet!), come to the Faerie server and take in a performance. The Firebird Theatre puts on a creative, emotionally enthralling, and expertly-performed live theatre show that should not be missed by any Eorzean.

Their next production is The Simple Life of Johanna Cadieu , and this is their first completely original show they are putting on. While it does not have a performance calendar set yet, the troupe will be recruiting volunteers to help with this production through their official Discord . And as for me, I know I will certainly be there opening night.

items.title: Wisdom of Nym: Melee weaponry Final Fantasy XIV could use for future jobs
items.summary: So let's recap. Last week, I posited something that I feel is pretty straightforward: We're hitting a point where clearly we can no longer rely on past jobs as a particularly strong guidepost for future jobs in Final Fantasy XIV. Not in the sense that we're going to stop getting new jobs (that seems highly [...]
items.content:
So let’s recap. Last week, I posited something that I feel is pretty straightforward: We’re hitting a point where clearly we can no longer rely on past jobs as a particularly strong guidepost for future jobs in Final Fantasy XIV . Not in the sense that we’re going to stop getting new jobs (that seems highly unlikely) but in the sense that I do not feel confident in looking back at prior jobs and saying, “Ah, yes, the hint suggests our next job will be Geomancer.” This doesn’t mean it’s best to not bother making guesses any longer, and indeed, I think there are a number of things we can look toward as potential guides moving forward.

Last week, I talked about magical arts that the game could explore. This week? We’re covering melee weapons. Unfortunately, in some ways this covers a whole lot less ground, since there’s not as much to talk about in some senses and our first new job reveal has made it very clear that the designers are willing to just make up new weapons if they want. In other ways, it’s more fun, since human beings have a truly staggering number of ways to hurt one another within arm’s reach. So let’s talk about it.

No, I am not saying that a future job will use a car as a melee weapon. Although now that I write that, it would be cool… but no, no, stay focused. I’m talking about whips. We all talk about whips because whips are dope, but there is actually a decent history of whips as a weapon in the series as a whole, and the fun thing is that they’re also usually used in weird ways.

Let’s be real, some weapons presuppose a job. If you’re going to have a katana, you’re going to have Samurai in the game. But whips tend to be associated with more unique individual characters. Sometimes casters, frequently hybrid casters, often characters who have a mishmash of different abilities and are clearly meant as a repository for a whole bunch of series stuff in one person because it wouldn’t fit together otherwise. I mentioned whips a few times discussing Beastmaster as they would have made sense for the job, but there are also plenty of other conceptual jobs where they’d also work fine.

What’s the downside? Well, as cool as whips are, they’re a bit of a bastard to animate. And as mentioned, there isn’t really one solid set of concepts that fits around them, so whatever it was would be more or less original. Still cool, though.

Now, I’ve speculated on hammers more than a few times, and it’d be fair to point out that at this point Warrior has a few hammers. I definitely think that the odds of a very heavily mace-focused job have gone down. But the fact is that it’s still out there, and we’ve even got a couple of NPCs using a hammer as a weapon. To be blunt, there’s room for this.

What precise role these weapons would serve is up for debate, of course; you could pair maces with tanks (and indeed, Nero takes up a similar role) but you could also make the argument to have them as a DPS. (Surely it hasn’t slipped anyone’s notice that DPS jobs tend to be more fast and agile with their weaponry, yes?) The major downside is simply what I already noted. Both Dark Knight and Warrior already have the “slow, weighty weapon” category rather well filled, and it’d thus be harder to find a new way to make this feel unique regardless of its role… and when dealing with a big, heavy mace, you expect slow, weighty weapons as a matter of course.

It’s kind of funny, at least to me, that this series has multiple different weapons that are all broadly categorized as “a stick.” We’ve got staves, and we have rods, so what’s the difference with poles? The answer is clear to anyone who has played Final Fantasy XII or Final Fantasy Tactics , and that’s that we talking not about wizardly objects but about twirling poles that are used to poke, smack, trip, and generally pummel things into submission. These are your classic thwackin’ stick.

Poles aren’t exactly common through the series, and usually they don’t show up in favor of mage staves. In fact, one of their most prominent appearances is within the aforementioned FFT , where a big part of their strength lay in the fact that they are magically balanced and thus surprisingly capable melee weapons within the hands of mages. But that’s part of the fun. They can work in a remarkable number of contexts and can work well as a weapon for a martial arts job without using knuckles or for something else more lightly armored.

Of course, the flip side is that we’re talking about a franchise where two things are true. First, there are not actually a lot of different martial artists who don’t fit under the “punch stuff” header, and second, if the game were going to give us a mage that could mix it up in melee, we’d be right to say, “Isn’t that Red Mage?” And yes. It is Red Mage. So, again, this would be a bit of a “starting from scratch” for the character concept. Not that there aren’t potential jobs that could fit here anyway, but let’s move on.

“Wait a second. We have swords. We have so many kinds of sword!” And yes, we do, please sit down for a second. I am not saying that a new job will be released that is just Paladin Againadin with another sword. I’m saying that there are a lot of types of sword, as evidenced by the fact that we currently have many jobs using swords already, and the addition of skyltborg should make it clear that you can just call a new kind of shield whatever you want.

Now, the obvious reason to add a new kind of sword would be to add a job that traditionally uses a sword as a weapon. And to be clear, there are a couple of those; Mystic Knight/Rune Fencer/etc. is an obvious candidate (and vaguely hinted at with the Corvosi swordmaster in the variant dungeon). But I include this here partly as a bit of a joke so that both of these columns have four entries and partly because there are a lot of sword-adjacent weapons that could wind up called in. Serah Farron got a transforming sword-bow because the developers wanted her to have a special weapon, and I’m not going to suggest we’ll get that as a whole thing; I’m suggesting that having a new kind of sword variant is a long tradition in this series, so we should never discount the possibility of Yet Another Sword.

I mean, heck, by that token, Endwalker and presumably Evercold will be the only expansions that add a new job without some kind of sword variant. Yes, gunblades count here.

Feedback, as always, is welcome in the comments down below or via mail to eliot@massivelyop.com . Next week, I have four more melee weapons to go over like I mentioned, so let’s continue along this particular garden path.

items.title: Diesel x Final Fantasy XIV “BRAVE” Turns Eorzea Into a 27-Piece Fashion Collection
items.summary: Diesel x Final Fantasy XIV “BRAVE” transforms Eorzea into a 27-piece collection of denim, graphic apparel, silver jewelry, and collectible fashion.
items.content:
Fashion collaborations built around video games have become increasingly common, but familiarity has also raised the standard. Putting recognizable characters on a T-shirt can establish a connection between two brands quickly. Translating an expansive fictional universe into clothing that remains compelling without the source material is considerably more difficult. Diesel and Square Enix are attempting the latter with their new Final Fantasy XIV project.

Built around the shared concept of “BRAVE,” the collaboration centers on a 27-piece capsule spanning washed denim jackets, wide-leg denim trousers, hoodies, long-sleeve shirts, graphic T-shirts, and silver jewelry. Its references reach into the mythology and organizations of Final Fantasy XIV rather than concentrating exclusively on logos, drawing from Azem’s Crystal, the Mothercrystal, the Grand Companies of Eorzea, and members of the Scions of the Seventh Dawn including Y’shtola, Thancred, Alphinaud, and Estinien.

The project extends beyond clothing. An initial September 16, 2026 launch at Isetan Shinjuku in Tokyo introduces customization through job-icon embroidery alongside a 30-set limited Scions of the Seventh Dawn Complete Box. A wider release follows October 2 through Diesel’s online store and DIESEL SHIBUYA, with additional pop-ups planned at Hankyu Umeda in Osaka and Iwataya in Fukuoka. DIESEL ART GALLERY in Shibuya will simultaneously expand the collaboration into contemporary art through a Kosuke Kawamura exhibition running from October 2 through November 8.

That breadth matters. Diesel x Final Fantasy XIV is not treating gaming as a convenient graphic theme. It is building a small cultural ecosystem around a fictional world whose audience has spent years developing relationships with its characters, locations, symbols, and communities.

The strongest collaborations usually begin with an idea more substantial than audience overlap.

Final Fantasy XIV is fundamentally structured around courage expressed through action. Players enter dangerous environments, develop characters through increasingly demanding roles, form parties, confront seemingly impossible enemies, and progress through a narrative built around responsibility, sacrifice, loyalty, and perseverance.

Diesel approaches bravery from another direction.

The Italian brand has spent decades embracing provocation, irreverence, unconventional styling, distressed surfaces, exaggerated proportions, and an attitude toward denim that rarely depends on pristine presentation. Under its contemporary creative direction, that willingness to make fashion slightly uncomfortable or visually disruptive has remained central to the brand’s relevance.

Those definitions of bravery are obviously not identical.

That is precisely what makes the concept useful.

Instead of pretending a fashion label and MMORPG naturally occupy the same creative territory, “BRAVE” identifies a philosophical point of contact while allowing each side to retain its own language.

Final Fantasy XIV provides designers with an unusually deep source archive.

The MMORPG has grown across years of storytelling, expansions, characters, locations, factions, jobs, weapons, creatures, symbols, and recurring visual motifs. For fashion, that density creates possibilities far beyond conventional character merchandise.

The Diesel collection draws from several levels of that mythology.

items.title: Diesel and ‘Final Fantasy XIV’ Channel a “Brave” Spirit for Their Collaborative Capsule
Wisdom of Nym: Magical concepts that Final Fantasy XIV could potentially use for new jobs
items.summary: I'm going to open this particular column - which itself is going to lead into a series of columns - with a statement that may be controversial but may not. items.content:
I’m going to open this particular column – which itself is going to lead into a series of columns – with a statement that may be controversial but may not. I think we have reached the point with Final Fantasy XIV at which strict readings of former jobs are no longer actually useful in terms of speculation on future jobs.

Don’t get me wrong, my point here is not “how are they going to make new jobs.” That’s not actually difficult. My point is that we have gone through the common jobs and then the uncommon jobs and then the obscure jobs and we are now into the Weird Zone. You’re left with jobs like Green Mage, a job that has never shown up in a single mainline title and actually has only a single game where it’s a distinct job of any sort, and that’s one of the stronger options.

That means that we’re now at a point where we need to look at weapons or concepts to fill things out in terms of speculation. And hey, these do exist in some abundance… starting with magic because it’s a place where, really, weaponry doesn’t matter. You can come up with something , even something weird, for most of these jobs. The main concept isn’t about the weapon but about the kind of magic that these jobs wield.

We do, in fact, have a pretty clear picture of what Geomancers are in broad strokes; they’re the Far East version of Conjurers, and so it could be said that this idea is pointless because that’s White Mage. But the thing is that White Mage has, increasingly, moved from the feel of nature mage into the domain of being an explicit cleric. Geomancy is something different, and it wouldn’t exactly break the world to find out that there’s a separate wing of Geomancy that expands beyond where the conjury-adjacent version stops.

If there’s any drawback here, it’s the fact that this is an established form of magic, and you have to make Geomancers feel different from Conjurers. I imagine if we were still in a world where we got multiple advanced jobs from base jobs, Geomancer would make sense as a damage fork from Conjurer. That time is so over it never really began. But it’d be wrong to pretend that Geomancy as its own thing doesn’t have some legs to it.

Necromancy is weird in the Final Fantasy franchise as a whole. The concept is present in lots of games, but there is basically only one game where you can actually play as the job, and even that is only as a bonus element added in re-releases. We know Necromancers exist in this game, but we cannot become Necromancers. And that makes some sense; in these universes, Necromancy just being an evil art would kind of preclude it being something that players can do.

Still, one of the points I’m making here is that we’re starting to run up to a level where there are not that many more options that are totally new. Saying that you can finally become a Necromancer as a heroic option also wouldn’t be coming out of nowhere, even if I feel like it’s not going to happen for a bit to come. If and when we go to the Void it would make sense, though…

Let’s be clear here: “Green plant life magic” is not something that is usually given a whole lot of thought in this series, either. It comes up in various places, but not really as a combat discipline (it’s a big deal with Final Fantasy XII’s Viera, but it isn’t part of their combat arts). I suspect some of the people who are eager for Green Mage as a concept think that’s what it is when, by and large, this is not a concept that exists in a lot of games in the franchise.

But it is a concept that exists a lot in several adjacent franchises, perhaps notable being the Seiken Densetsu/Mana series that sits just off to the left. It’s distinct from Geomancy as a concept in that it’s less concerned with weather and the natural elements and more with life and nature as a whole.

An awful lot of spin-off titles love dropping in bonus jobs that have psionic abilities in there somewhere, right down to having a somewhat unified pseudo-future aesthetic that, let’s be real, would not look out of place in Solution Nine. That’s not why I’m bringing this up, though; I’m bringing it up because you will note I just said this comes up a heck of a lot in later titles and spin-offs as a bonus feature. And we are into “bonus feature” territory with jobs now, so let’s psion up.

You may argue that essentially, psionics are not magic and do not work like magic is supposed to. To that I say you are not going to care too much about the fine details of the execution as long as you get some kind of job that has a unified theme and features psionic darts or throwing things. Let’s not front.

A lot of the visuals between psionics and illusions wind up being similar if not overlapping, but in this case I think the difference is very meaningful because while psionics have some language in the series, illusionists have less. But that’s not to say the idea is foreign to the game in any way. Let’s be real: Illusionists, Necromancers, and Wizards are the three most fundamental “types” of caster from D&D and points related, and while you can definitely identify the third and the second just doesn’t tend to be playable, the first rarely comes up. But there’s a lot of potential material there.

You could argue that illusion doesn’t make much sense as a raw damage or healing job, and there’s some weight to that, but my point here is not to interrogate the mechanics but point out that this could work. Put it this way, if a new job has an illusionary magic focus and it involves leaving ghostly afterimages that explode into magical damage, that’s illusions even if mechanically it’s more direct than the name might suggest.

In older games, things like Black Wizards existed as straight upgrades to Black Mages. In other games, you get jobs like Arithmetician or some of the weirder jobs in Final Fantasy X-2 . The point here is that we are talking about metamagic as a concept. Rather than being a mage that has its own unique magical discipline, it’s a mage that yoinks two or more other disciplines and combines them in a new way.

items.title: Review: Final Fantasy XIV on Nintendo Switch 2 is the best version of the game
items.content:
I have wanted to get back into Final Fantasy XIV for quite some time. I am a massive fan of everything it offers, from the art direction to the scope of the world and adventures that are held within it. I love the way that it handles narrative within the MMO format, and the massive range of locations to visit. I really, really love the music (I went to a FFXIV symphony and everything), and just generally the very Final Fantasy design of it.

Related reading: To think that I played this for the first time way back on the PlayStation 3. My thoughts back then.

But – and it’s a big but – Final Fantasy XIV is a MMO, and MMOs do demand a time commitment, both in terms of the raw hours you plug into it, and the frequency with which you need to play. Take a big break from an MMO, and it just becomes progressively more difficult to step back into.

I tried to get back into FFXIV once when I first picked up the ROG Xbox Ally . The device handled the game just lovely, but I’m not a frequent PC player, and so at some point I put the device down, took a long break, and just… let my subscription slip again.

I am, however, a frequent Nintendo Switch 2 player. By that I mean “daily”. And so now, with the game’s little icon sitting right there on my Switch 2 home screen, I’ve been logging in for at least a little playtime every day. I’ve already made significantly more progress than I did on the ROG.

Final Fantasy XIV plays just lovely on Switch 2, to start with that important point. The console’s screen is just large enough to be able to handle the very busy interface (it’s an MMO, it’s necessary) without distracting from the core action when you want to watch the fireworks. The game’s visual engine is just now ever-so-slightly showing its age with relatively primitive character models and textures – it has been going for something like 13 years at this point – but the art direction is still as stunning as ever, and I’ve loved revisiting my favourite parts of the world from my first playthrough.

Speaking of, I have started a totally fresh character and save file (I wouldn’t even be able to track down my original avatar from a decade ago, if she still exists on servers somewhere, even if I wanted to. I can’t remember my username, password, or the email address it was attached to). I love how it’s possible to play through all the base game and early expansions with NPCs, and not rely on parties of humans for the various dungeons. If you’ve ever played a FFXIV dungeon before, you’ll know that human allies tend to… well, race through it. One of the few unpleasant memories I have from my first playthrough of Final Fantasy XIV was getting to the very final dungeon of the base game and basically missing the whole thing (and being left behind) because I was trying to follow the story. The conclusion to literally dozens of hours of play.

Now, thanks to NPCs, you can enjoy most of the many expansions and all the stories within them at your own pace. And enjoy the typically excellent music, enemy layouts and dungeon design without feeling rushed, too. I even took time to take screenshots, which is one of my favourite ways to log my adventures in this game.

There is a downside, though. Because Square Enix wants to funnel players into the later expansions where, from their perspective, all the value to the players is, they’ve taken steps to streamline the earlier parts of the game, meaning that you accumulate experience points much (much) faster, and have to do far (far) fewer quests along the way. I have been exclusively undertaking the main quest line, with no side quests, let alone grinding, and my avatar is more than twice the minimum recommended level for any given quest or boss battle.

I understand why they did this, because otherwise it would be a truly intimidating, overwhelming task for a completely new player to get up to the newer expansions, but it means that those same players don’t get to spend enough time in parts of the world to really enjoy their contribution to the whole. The major cities are fine, but you’ll fly through little town areas where previously you’d spend a gaming session or two completing all the side quests. They’re barely blips and blink-and-you’ll-miss-them moments now, which really messes with the pacing for what was previously a truly wonderfully paced game that slowly walked you from one wonder to the next.

I don’t necessarily know what the solution is there, though if it were possible, I would have appreciated the option to toggle whether I wanted the accelerating levelling on or not.

Still, that’s my only gripe. The only other minor issue is that, when it comes to the chat, the Switch’s virtual keyboard doesn’t exactly allow for the same typing speed as a proper keyboard. I don’t even know if it’s possible to connect a Bluetooth keyboard to the Switch 2, as I haven’t tried yet, but even if it were possible, that would significantly undermine the portability of the experience. Currently I haven’t been social enough in FFXIV to require the chat function much, but I can see that becoming an issue later on in the game.

Those are only minor quibbles, obviously, set against a game that is hundreds upon hundreds of hours in scope, and now in an extremely portable and accessible format. FFXIV is a hobby all by itself, and now I can embrace and indulge it in full.

items.title: Wisdom of Nym: The cross(over) to bear in Final Fantasy XIV’s upcoming raids for Evercold
items.summary: Thanks to the most recent fan festival, Square Enix has confirmed that Final Fantasy XIV is getting not one but two crossover raid series in the Evercold patch sequence. Both our alliance raid and normal raid will be crossovers with other properties. This sucks! I am not happy about that! I also am happy about it and [...]
items.content:
Thanks to the most recent fan festival, Square Enix has confirmed that Final Fantasy XIV is getting not one but two crossover raid series in the Evercold patch sequence. Both our alliance raid and normal raid will be crossovers with other properties. This sucks! I am not happy about that! I also am happy about it and I don’t really care. Which is to say that mostly, on a personal level, my current reaction to this news is the same as being told that the next raid series will feature mechanics .

This is a true fact, but it is in and of itself a value-neutral statement. At the same time, I can understand why someone would look at this news and react with an “aw, nerts ” just like I can understand why someone would be hype about this. So my goal with this week’s column is strike a middle tone for mutual understanding without reducing anything or diminishing complaints. And let’s start by acknowledging that FFXIV has always been using this stuff for crossovers.

The very first alliance raid series was the Crystal Tower, which itself is a direct lift of several portions of Final Fantasy III’s ending sequence. And this isn’t a minor lift, either! Emperor Xande is a major figure in game lore and also is lifted directly from FFIII , whole cloth. Then Stormblood brought us another crossover raid, ditto Shadowbringers , and ditto again with Dawntrail . Two-thirds of the alliance raids have been crossovers.

“But normal raids traditionally haven’t!” Sort of true, yeah. I mean, obviously that’s not true of Omega, where the first two wings were express crossovers and Omega itself is a direct pull from Final Fantasy V . And it’s not really true of the Eden series, which is filled with direct nods to Final Fantasy VIII right down to its structure as a love story. It’s less common, but it is not exactly unheard of . And again, I want to be clear here when I stress that this frequently involves crossover elements that aren’t just throwaway moments but major parts of ongoing lore within the game.

However… I think that’s also something that’s worth citing there: While I am being accurate when I say these things are crossovers (because they are), I’m also eliding that there are crossovers and then there are crossovers .

In the Ivalice series, we see a sequence of events unfold that make it clear Ivalice is a place on Etheirys, complete with history and lore that ties into the setting as we already know it. We can tie parts of Garlean history back to Goug, and the implication is not that Goug is a location in a different world that has been slammed into our world but a place in this world.

By contrast, the NieR: Automata crossover is explicitly a crossover. There is no implication that the world of NieR is connected in any meaningful way with the First, just that these two things overlapped for a time. 2B is the same character from the actual game. And that’s a bit of a different proposition. This is not the marriage of elements from one thing into another but an explicit cross between two otherwise separate properties, and the reality is that this is a significantly different situation requiring a different consideration.

Now, I do not have the space in this column to explain why crossovers are the way they are (it’d honestly be a stretch even in a Storyboard), but the topline takeaway is this: unless you are the Kingdom Hearts series, the fact of the matter is that both halves of the crossover need to take place in a bubble where nothing of significance can happen in either direction. And this is going to be the case in Evercold as well, regardless of what actually happens in the crossovers.

Let’s use the Evangelion crossover as an example: Either it takes place in the middle of the series somewhere (in which case it can’t actually change anything about its characters because the series already exists), or it takes place after the ending (in which case it can’t actually change anything about its characters because they already reached the end of their character arcs). This means the goal is to have you just stand in the same place while saying, “Wow, it’s nice to meet you, Shinji Ikari from the hit anime Neon Genesis Evangelion,” which doesn’t provide much in the way of compelling plot points.

And even beyond the natural plot cul-de-sac, there’s the simple reality that in order to be excited about a Final Fantasy VII crossover, you need to be just as much of a fan of FFXIV and FFVII and want to see the two of them in the same space at the same time. That’s not a given. I am a very big fan of Mystery Science Theater 3000; that does not mean that I want a sequence of content in which my FFXIV character travels to the Satellite of Love and has to do a bunch of raids in which the bots riff on me every time I get a vuln-up stack.

Well, now I sort of do, but not as a serious story element.

So there are plenty of reasons to look at this and feel kind of disappointed, especially in the wake of how the Arcadion was an oustanding story. Why wouldn’t I be even a little disappointed by the fact that two major story arcs are going to be dedicated to crossovers? Because it’s not just about “how many of these things have been crossovers anyway.” Another big element is just the reality of “I haven’t actually seen the story yet.”

The NieR: Automata crossover is bad as a story, but it’s bad because it is bad . The crossover elements don’t help , but the Vana’diel series is also an explicit crossover and that story is… good! It’s pretty fun! Not perfect, but it all works! And it’s especially important to keep this in mind because alliance raids and normal raids are a combination of multiple elements working in concert.

Pandæmonium’s story was bad. But the actual fights? Those were good and fun. Myths of the Realm had some major issues with its story but not with the execution of its fights or rewards. At this point, I’d argue the Void Ark series has a fine story, but it’s mechanically a complete forking mess. I’m not going to get too far out over my skis when it is entirely possible for the story side to have issues while the gameplay is good.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV Online – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition Review
items.summary: If you haven’t heard of Final Fantasy XIV by now, where have you been? This hugely popular MMO has been around for more than ten years now and is
items.content:
If you haven’t heard of Final Fantasy XIV by now, where have you been? This hugely popular MMO has been around for more than ten years now and is currently awaiting its sixth expansion, Evercold, in January 2027. Another development that you might have missed, but one that I was feverishly excited about, was the release of the fan-favourite game on the Nintendo Switch 2.

I’ve had some time with the game on Switch 2 recently; in fact, I’ve been playing Final Fantasy XIV exclusively on the platform for the last couple of weeks for my daily level grinds. I have developed thoughts about it.

Let’s get the bad things out of the way first. Yes, it does suck quite considerably that you must get a separate subscription alongside your main one (if you have one). Sure, this is at a reduced price if you have another subscription, but it does feel very cheeky. If Switch 2 is going to be your only means of playing FFXIV, however, this is an irrelevant criticism. I will pay for both, but I’m like this.

Also, this is a chunky game, as you would expect from 100s of hours of gameplay. Even if you only do the Free Trial, which runs from A Realm Reborn up to Shadowbringers, that totals around 170 hours for just the main content. As such, it totals a whopping 117GB, which is a VERY large amount of the Switch 2’s system storage. I’ve got into the habit of removing things from the console, but if you don’t, you might want to get deleting if you’re considering diving into Eorzea.

Outside of these general critiques, I did initially have problems with the keybindings when playing the game. The A button on Switch is “confirm” on Switch 2, which is conveniently in the same place as the “cancel” button on PlayStation. So, my dumb ass kept deselecting the boss and/or party members as I was trying to do the Arcadion. But a quick switch of those in the system settings has helped my muscle memory not flare up continually.

Additionally, I must admit that things can be a little small on the Switch 2’s screen in handheld mode. This is easily remedied – of course – by altering the size of the UI details in the settings. But just a heads up that, if you copy across your settings from other platforms, like I did, you will have to spend some time changing things before you can legibly see what’s on the screen.

Believe it or not, that’s it for negatives. The short story is that it runs astonishingly well on the Switch 2. Across a variety of content, except Savage Raids as I am currently in search of a new static, there was no noticeable difference for me in performance between PlayStation 5 and Switch 2. The only issue was with the load times on occasion, but the delay with loading after revival in combat has already been repaired in a hot fix.

This is the case in both handheld and docked too, with few noticeable differences in performance between the two. The only times I saw anything close to struggling was loading into busy areas such as Limsa Lominsa in handheld mode, but even then, the drops in performance were barely noticeable. This does make sense, of course, because the game originally ran on the PlayStation 3. But it’s nonetheless impressive.

Also, if different control methods are your thing (no judgement here), the Switch 2 version of the game supports the mouse mode for easy clicking around targets. This eases up one of the biggest problems with playing on a controller, which is being able to select things outside of the key cyclable options. This is not a problem in most instances. But if you’re a Healer in an Alliance Raid with some – ahem – lacklustre Healers in other parties, you will know the struggle.

As are the visuals too. These have been brought down a touch to fit onto the platform, resulting in a graphical downgrade from PlayStation 5 to Switch 2, just not one that’s as severe as I was expecting. The soft purple hues of the trees near the Crystarium, the colourful lanterns of Kugane, and the tragic beauty of Ultima Thule are all present and accounted for. The game is just as beautiful as it’s ever been, just on a smaller screen.

Joseph Bradford Posted: Aug 13, 2026 4:00 PM ET Category: Previews 0

The Switch 2's upgraded Nvidia-powered chip powers experiences like Cyberpunk 2077 at actually playable framerates; an MMO that originally launched on the PlayStation 3 should be no real issue.

The question I had was whether the experience would feel good when the Switch 2 was undocked, untethered by both a possible wired internet connection and the extra juice the dock helps enable from the hardware. And I'm delighted to say that it is so much better than I ever expected.

Final Fantasy XIV brought all of the massive MMO to the Nintendo Switch 2 last week in what they are calling an early access launch to test the servers. The same process played out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles when the MMO was ported, but with the extra subscription fee required as part of the Nintendo tax, it is nice to check it out on the console before the sub fee kicks in next month.

So, it should be noted that when using the Switch 2 handheld, the console is locked to 30fps. This honestly is fine, which is wild for me to be saying that as someone who thinks that in the Year of our Lord Two-Thousand Twenty Six everything should be 60fps minimum. And I will admit, I know I would enjoy it even more if it was.

But when I learned it would be a 30fps lock while undocked, I was pretty afraid it would feel bad. But after hours and hours playing through some of Endwalker and running Duties to level my Pictomancer, I have to say it hasn't bothered me at all.

When docked, the framerate is capable of running at 60, though it does dip in busy areas, like the market at Limsa Lominsa. Running around Thavnair brought what feels like framerates in the 40s, which is fine, though I do appreciate that there is an option to just lock the FPS to 30 on TV as well for that consistent framerate if that's what you want.

YouTube channel GVG has a good breakdown of the full metrics, so I would definitely check out the embed above for more accurate data (since we don't have our own framerate analysis tool). Suffice to say, this might be the first game I've played in a long while where I am willing to play at 30fps, especially if it means I can play while lounging in bed, unshackled from my TV or PC.

One of the most exciting parts of launching an MMO on a new platform is the influx of new players it brings into the community. I've been running around with a level 30 Paladin on the Ultros server, and the early game areas feel busy. One of the things I've always liked about Final Fantasy XIV is that early game locations never simply felt like ghost towns, so even during lulls in content, there are always players going around doing class quests, doing dailies, and so much more. With so many new players, these regions feel even more alive when I'm in them.

It's also been exciting seeing friends and colleagues of mine who either tried FFXIV and bounced off it in the past find their way back into Eorzea, or those friends of mine I've tried to convince to play with me finally jumping in for the first time. The legendary free trial is doing a lot of heavy lifting here, but it's so worth it to convince friends who have a Switch 2 and have been curious what all the acclaim was about to hop in and run with you.

Perhaps Final Fantasy XIV's greatest stregnth is the cross-play/cross-progression the MMO has always operated with. I have a serious aversion to playing alts in MMOs, so one of the things that drew me to FFXIV was the fact that no matter where I played, it was the same character. The Job system was also a major draw. I despise starting over in MMOs, so being able to just do everything on one character has been my dream (and one I really, really wish more MMOs would just copy at this point).

The Nintendo Switch 2 makes this feel even better, and I can't quite explain why. There is something about playing the MMO on my Steam Machine in my office and then just curling up in bed with the Switch 2 in handheld mode, picking up Endwalker from where I left off.

I am seriously never going to catch up to a current expansion, it seems.

The Switch 2 version gives some interesting ways to play the MMO, though. You can take advantage of the console's weird Joy-Con 2 Mouse mode and almost match the feel of playing on the PC. Personally, I don't like this. I use a controller on PC anyways as it is, but this necessitates clicking skills for the most part while in combat, and it never quite felt good enough to make it worth messing with beyond professional curiosity.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV is perfect for the Switch 2
items.summary: Though it has its ups and downs
items.content:
Final Fantasy XIV coming to the Switch 2 is a dream come true for me; one of my favorite games now in a portable form factor. I’ve put a ton of time into the game on the system, testing just about every scenario I can think of outside of becoming a streamer and having a crowd of people follow me everywhere. Overall, I’m pretty happy with the port and can recommend it to players new and old, but I certainly wouldn’t abandon PC for this version.

The thing I and most others were curious about most was performance on Switch 2. I have bad news on that front, as you’re pretty much never going to get 60 frames per second on Switch 2 outside of certain cutscenes and exactly one area in one dungeon. It’s disappointing there’s no performance mode or anything, but you can cap your framerate to 30 in Docked Mode for more stability. Portable is also capped at 30, so you’re essentially getting parity with that aside from resolution. Your framerate can and will still dip below 30 in some situations, like running around a crowded Limsa Lominsa, but Limsa ‘tis a silly place. You can hear more about performance in this short:

As for visuals, the game looks good. Not amazing; there’s a lot of aliasing, and you can definitely tell the resolution is lower when going from 1440p or 4K on PC, but good. Resolution often screws with your custom HUD setup, which is something I was worried about here, but aside from needing to increase the chatbox font and move my job gauges a bit to the right, I was able to download my configs no problem. It moves seamlessly between portable and docked modes as well, something this version has over playing the PC version on Steam Deck.

Steam Deck might be able to hit higher framerates more consistently, but Switch 2 has it soundly beat in convenience and battery life, not to mention fan noise. I gave up playing the game on Steam Deck after Dawntrail launched, as just playing the game made my Deck scream in agony and it would go from full battery to almost dead very, very quickly. That’s at the lowest possible settings and with a lower resolution than Switch 2 offers. FFXIV will still drain the Switch 2 pretty quickly, but it’s far from the worst I’ve seen on the platform. Just make sure you don’t register for a duty at like 30% battery and you’re fine, or have your docked setup nearby.

Being able to go from portable to docked seamlessly here is fantastic, though the star of the show here really is portable mode. I love being able to do my dailies and slowly get every Job to cap while sitting on my couch, talking with my family, or just not sitting at my PC. Especially with the weather being so hot and my bedroom, where my computer lives, is basically an oven. I could even play outside on the porch if going outside wouldn’t melt me.

One of the best parts of portable mode is the touch screen. Sometimes navigating certain menus is just more convenient with a mouse-like setup, and just being able to touch the screen makes it super easy. In Docked mode, you can use either one of the Joy-Con 2 as a mouse, but I find this feature leaves a lot to be desired; both when you’re using it and even when you’re not. Playing with split Joy-Con 2, I found my fingers would often activate the mouse sensor, messing up my controls for a second or two. Playing with mouse mode… You just don’t have enough buttons to actually play the game unless you’re the kind of person who likes to click on their hotbar actions. You could plug in a Keyboard and just use one of the Joy-Con 2 as a mouse, which does allow for a left-handed mouse setup, but at that point you might as well just plug in an actual MMO mouse while you’re at it.

Another point of contention is that there’s no physical release. That’s not a big deal for Final Fantasy XIV as it hasn’t actually been on a disc in a long time, but on Switch 2 storage space is at a premium. Final Fantasy XIV will take up almost half of your console’s onboard storage at 108 GB. With Evercold on the Horizon, it’s only going to get bigger too. I actually bought a new microSD card specifically for this game, and am working on putting together a faux physical copy, complete with a game box and “cartridge” to store the SD card in. With… everything getting so expensive lately, I settled on a 256 GB card, so I’ll have to swap out the SD card to play my other Switch 2 games, which is inconvenient. You could simply keep FFXIV on your onboard storage and all other games on an SD card, which was recommended when the game launched as there were loading issues with the SD card, but I prefer to have at least some variety.

As of writing and most likely as of when you read this, Square Enix is offering all Switch 2 players a free month of the game. After that ends, you’ll need to pay an additional subscription fee to play on Switch 2 and other platforms like PC and PS5. If you just play on Switch 2, you simply pay the normal sub, but if, for example, you want to swap between PC and Switch 2 you’ll have to pay an additional half of the subscription each month. This is done through a weird currency obfuscation method Square Enix calls FFXIV Coins. You buy coins, then use them to pay for the sub.

First off, why the obfuscation? I’d really rather you just tell me up front what it costs without me having to translate and convert. There’s a reason Nintendo and Microsoft got rid of their points systems on their storefronts. Second, I know this is how Square got out of requiring players to need Nintendo Switch Online to play on Switch 2… but personally I already pay for NSO every year, and it’s overall cheaper than this weird Coin model; $50 a year for the Expansion Pak version as opposed to $70 a year by my math. That $70 doesn’t include an already existing subscription to FFXIV, by the way; that’s just on top of playing on Switch 2. I haven’t actually paid for my sub in a long time (thanks for literally paying my sub, Square!), but if I were to stop writing about FFXIV, I would be concerned about that additional cost. Being subscribed to NSO does get you an additional free teleport destination in-game… but I have teleport tickets; I don’t need that. It’s quite literally useless to me. In this situation, I’d probably just pick what I’m going to play on for that month: Switch 2 or PC.

Seeing as the Switch 2 version feels more like a nice supplement to me, I’d go with PC most of the time. In between MSQ patches, sure, I’ll take Switch 2, but if I go back to raiding or when there’s more story to play, I’d prefer the higher fidelity and framerate of my PC. I hope Square and Nintendo reconsider the choice of FFXIV Coin, because if they did, I’d shill this version as much as humanly possible. I mean, I’ll still do that for the game overall, but here I’d mostly recommend the free trial, then moving over to PC or being absolutely sure you want to play on Switch 2 forever. If FFXIV Coin wasn’t a thing, then you’d bet your sweet bippy I’d buy every expansion twice (read: once, thanks again Square!) so I could play on both platforms. For right now though, I’m pretty dang happy with this version.

items.summary: New Playable Content, FINAL FANTASY VII Remake Trilogy Crossover Raid Series, Nintendo Switch™ 2 Version Release Date and More Announced at FAN FESTIVAL 2026 in Berlin Keynote Address
items.content:
London (25 th July, 2026) – SQUARE ENIX® today revealed brand-new information about Evercold , the sixth expansion for its critically acclaimed MMORPG FINAL FANTASY XIV Online , set to launch in January 2027 alongside new playable content, a FINAL FANTASY VII Remake Trilogy crossover raid series, the Nintendo Switch 2 version release date and more. An extended teaser trailer for Evercold was also revealed, providing a glimpse into the world of the Fourth and the adventures that await the Warrior of Light in the start of the Goddless Realms Saga story arc. The extended Evercold teaser trailer is available at: https://youtu.be/urDT_At-AX4 During the Fan Festival 2026 in Berlin keynote address, Producer and Director Naoki Yoshida revealed the first new job coming to Evercold : Bastion—a main tank that wields a pair of greatshields known as skyltborg—and unveiled a trailer showcasing the new job in action. View the Bastion job trailer at: https://youtu.be/uaZlrprwSq4 Details were also shared on several new features coming to Evercold, including changes to the narrative structure that will be implemented for the main scenario, field, and game system, allowing players more freedom to choose what area they complete first between various paths in the main scenario. Through Auto Content Balancing, difficulty scaling and enemy levels will adjust to the appropriate player level as they play through dungeons in their chosen order. Additionally, a first look was provided for Character Action Skins, a feature that lets players assign alternate animations to personalize existing General actions, such as Teleport and Warp, with support for additional skins such as job actions arriving in future updates. Character customization will also be expanded so players have more ways to make their character stand out, including a greater range of color options with the new color picker, the ability to fine-tune features such as eyes and lips, new elements such as eye shadow, and more. Following the reveal of the EVANGELION - Ghosts of Desire alliance raid series in April, Yoshida unveiled a new teaser trailer and announced that acclaimed director and animator Mahiro Maeda will join the project as a special guest artist and designer. Throughout his career, Maeda has contributed to numerous acclaimed projects, including “Mad Max: Fury Road” (2015) as a concept artist and designer, and “EVANGELION:3.0 +1.0 THRICE UPON A TIME” (2021), where he served as director, concept art director, storyboard artist, art setting designer and key animator. Both development teams are working closely together to create an exciting new raid experience for players. To ensure server stability, there will be an approximately one-month free subscription period on Nintendo Switch 2. Whether beginning with the Free Trial, starting their adventure with the Starter Edition, or diving into the full story and experience with the Complete Edition, more players than ever before will soon be able to join together in the vast world of FINAL FANTASY XIV . More details are available at: https://sqex.to/Q0D06 An outline of the content reveals from the keynote address can be found below:

items.title: Sarah’s Final Fantasy XIV Fan Fest Experience
items.summary: What is the most magical event full of sparkle and wonder that only takes place every couple of years? Why, it's FFXIV FanFest! Sarah Ferries provides a journal of her experience at the event, including the Jollibee and Requiem Café visits.
items.content:
Let’s just start off by saying that the weather was way better in Los Angeles than the previous Fan Fests in Las Vegas. Yes, things like hotels were more expensive, but I would take that any day over the 100+-degree heat. Even Yoshi P (Producer and Director Naoki Yoshida) said he was melting!

I arrived about 8:30am for the 10am keynote to get a good seat. Just walking into the stage area, it felt a lot bigger than in previous years in Vegas. I was in my Pictomancer cosplay, which was a bit chilly, but better than being too hot. It did get warmer as the keynote went on, though. It truly was jam-packed and longer than a normal keynote. I was intending to post updates on social media like normal, but the internet was garbage inside the convention center so I just made notes on my phone, and was at least able to use Discord. That said, I also forgot to get the media-only WiFi information, so that’s partly on me.

Most of the keynote people loved. There was lots of cheering and clapping, especially with the Evercold trailer . However, when it came to showcasing the Reborn/Evolved modes, the people around me didn’t appear to like it, especially after Yoshi P announced that all new jobs will be only using the Evolved mode. I think it was the initial shock of changing things that really set people off, but after talking through it with people, it doesn’t seem like it’s going to be as big of a change as some people think. I was able to meet up with a lot of my friends from Twitch chats and Final Fantasy XIV, and after we all talked about it, I think it will be better. As someone who plays on a controller, this might be of particular benefit to me. I have my own rotation, and I have no idea if that’s the “correct” Pictomancer rotation, but with the evolved mode it might allow for more flexibility.

After the welcome ceremony, I went with a group of friends to Jollibee, which was holding a Final Fantasy XIV collaboration for Fan Fest. Even though the Roulette Game Show looked fun, we were all very hungry. We arrived at Jollibee and it fortunately wasn’t that busy. I think we only waited about a half hour. We wanted to go to this exact one, because we were told this was the only one that was fully decorated. I was amused at G’raha Tia being on the trash cans eating a sandwhich. This seemed to be the best time to go, since outside of Fan Fest people were saying that the lines at other times were many hours long. I got the $21 box to get my fancy emote. I only ate the sandwich there, but it was delicious. I really liked the sauce, and it came with the good reminder that no chocobos were harmed in the making of the food. We were wondering what they were going to do with the decorations after the event was over. I would’ve loved to take one of the aetheryte lights and put it in my room.

We made it back to Fan Fest around 3pm, and I wanted to see some of the developer panel to understand the Evolved mode a little better, but then I got distracted by shiny cosplayers and friends. Unfortunately, by around 4pm my feet hurt so bad I could not walk, which is partly the price I paid for wearing my cosplay shoes, and I ended up going back to my hotel to put on my sneakers before coming back. I was able to get back just in time to watch the “Glamoured to Life” cosplay walk for around twenty minutes before having to go to my meet and greet. I am glad I was able to see some of the streamers I watch walk, including my favorite scene I was able to see: Sultana drinking from the goblet on stage. The crowd reaction was great. She came out and pulled out the cup, at which point you could hear the gasps and the air leave the room. Then she went to drink, to which everyone immediately screamed, and then stood there for a second before giving a thumbs up. That got a lot of cheers.

When I got to my meet and greet, I am surprised how fast and easy it was. At bigger cons, these things are a mess and you often have to wait hours to meet your chosen guest. However, at Fan Fest you simply had to line up fifteen minutes before your appointment, and then go through relatively fast. I was able to meet Jason Charles Miller, who originally voiced Raubahn Aldynn in A Realm Reborn, but is perhaps better known for performing the vocals in the theme songs for Shadowbringers and Endwalker, plus “Unleashed” from Dawntrail . He was very nice and I even got to chat with him a little bit while my photo was taken.

The Piano Performance with Keiko and special guest Amanda Achen was out of this world. As always, Keiko has a beautiful princess dress for the performance. The sound and stage quality was fantastic. There were some camera issues, where the shot stayed on Keiko for a very long time even when Amanda was singing. I’m chalking that up to technical issues, hopefully. I’m so glad I was able to see the stage from my seat so I could see Amanda singing. Luckily, it wasn’t most of the concert, so I was able to watch the big screens on the sides of the stage.

I was able to attend a portion of “From Tacos to Tenders: Serving up the Lyrics of FFXIV ” with Michael-Christopher Koji Fox. The man is hilarious, and I love listening to him talk about the game, the antics, and how he comes up with lyrics. This panel showed how Square Enix really listens to its players as well as showcasing famous misheard lyrics to some of the songs from the game. One of the most misheard lyrics is from Ultima theme, with players chanting along with “big fat tacos” instead of “Beat, the Heart of Sabik.” Typing it out, it seems like a bizarre mishearing, but you’d have to hear it. He then had fans come up on stage to write new lyrics to “eScape”, which the audience voted on. The winning set of lyrics was actually changed for the Primals live concert at the end of the night! VTuber IronMouse was a special guest during this panel and gave a small concert at the end which was actually really good. I had never seen her before, but I liked her performance.

As much as I wanted to see random Q&As with Yoshi P, I hadn’t yet got the chance to play any of the games yet. I heard a lot of them were capping lines at 4:30, so wanted to get as much done as possible, though I am sad I missed the question about the butt slider.

I started with Run Alpaca Run, which is pretty much a carnival race horse game where you roll a ball into various holes: think of a mini version of Skee-Ball. I did not win, but it was still fun. I wasn’t able to get into the Crystalline Conflict Palaistra Challenge, as the line was already too long, and it’s not something I got into in-game, so it’s hard to compare the physical game to the digital area. I did try the Pelupelu Pitch, which is another carnival style game of ring toss. I am also terrible at this game and scored zero points, but it was still fun. Next was Mica’s Magical Maneuvers, which was a reaction-time based game. Sticks drop suddenly and you have to grab them before they hit the floor. Metem’s Limit Break Challenge was another carnival-style game I did not partake in, because of my tiny, sensitive hands. It gives participants one opening and a single punch to score big DPS; I watched a guy punch a score of 649, which was pretty high compared to the others. However, I did try the Arcadion Slam to try out for the Solution Nine Yans; shooting hoops with a basketball that couldn’t go wrong, right? Wrong! In my haste of trying to make baskets in competition with other people on a time limit, the ball bounced off the rim and hit me in the face. Luckily, it didn’t leave a bruise or a bloody nose, just hurt pride and some redness. Last but not least, Ride the Rhythm was the most popular game at Fan Fest. The line was always long, but it was definitely the highlight. This was basically a disco floor that people had to dance on, but with elements from a boss fight, complete with area of effect squares, tankbuster circles, and a stack marker. It was really cool to see boss mechanics from in the game come to life in person. There was one thing I didn’t get to do but I wish I had: the photo spot with G’raha Tia on a gondola. That was probably the second most popular thing at Fan Fest. I did get a photo at Aunt Tii’s Tacos in Tuliyollal, though.

Having Fan Fest modeled after the latest expansion, Dawntrail , and showcasing its main areas like Solution Nine and Tuliyollal was done really well. There were lots of photo opportunities with the giant “XIV” letters, well known landmarks like Aunt Tii’s Tacos, different Solution Nine areas such as a lounge and bar, and even a photo op with Honey B. Lovely, everyone’s favorite boss. (Alright, not everyone’s, but she was pretty popular.) The only thing I would’ve liked more of was an expanded Solution Nine lounge with more couches and chairs, as they were always full of people, meaning many had to sit along the walls or on the floor.

The last hurrah of the evening was a concert from The Primals, the official band of Final Fantasy XIV lead by Sound Director Masayoshi Soken since 2014. The members are Masayoshi Soken, Michael-Christopher Koji Fox, GUNN, Eikichi Iwai, and Tetsuya Tachibana. Last Fan Fest, people brought their own light sticks for the Primals concert and this year Square Enix decided to sell them at their merch station, which made it that much more fun and I was able to get one of the last light sticks before they sold out. There were multiple colors to choose from on the light stick to match the songs the Primals were playing, and everyone in the crowd seemed to be on the same page. The concert began with the “checking member status” display on the video screens, as one would see waiting for a dungeon to fill in game. The band began “Open Sky”, followed by “Scream”, “Ride the Rhythym”, “Not Afraid” (with special guest Yoshi P), “Unleashed”, “Shadowbringers”, “Absolute Tyranny”, “A Long Fall”, “Rise”, “eScape”, and finally “Under the Weight”. I was surprised when the concert ended as I was enjoying it so much I wasn’t ready for it to end.

Before I left Anaheim, I was able to visit the FFXIV Requiem Café. There was not a lot of merch left, and all the pastries and some of the drinks were sold out. I was able to grab a New Adventures drink, which had a sprout bookmark in the whipped cream atop a refreshing mint citrus soda, and the Scree! ice cream drink. This was a brown sugar milk tea with chocolate drizzle topped with a toasted marshmallow cold foam, gold lustre dust, and a serpent gummy. Both of these were VERY delicious. The inside of the café was magical and wondrous, with a fake giant tree that looked like a weeping willow with a few seats inside. It had a TV showing some story quests, as well as many cardboard stand ups of our favorite scions. The store was decked out with gaming computers that had the free trial loaded up for people to play the game, along with a post-it wall for gamers to leave their mark. I wish I could take the tree with me and put it in my house!

Overall this year’s Fan Fest was yards above the Las Vegas one in 2023. The weather was much nicer, there was a bigger space that was laid out much better, and there were better food options. As always, thank you Square Enix for putting on these events!
